A gripping start, then a sag about a quarter of the written reviews report, mostly through the comet half and its mutiny: 'chvilemi prilis preslapovala na miste', 'Prvni polovina je hodne pomala', 'celou prvni tretinu jsem mel problem se zacist', 'Tahne se to jako bolava noha'. One reader left it unfinished after a brilliant opening and three nearly quit, while many report no dull stretches ('Bez hluchych mist'); the lead stays active through the slow part, which Problém tří těles (DNF) did not have.

axis:density.note: About -2. Filler that several readers name, minutes of low-gravity jumping and a real-time talk of two friends getting drunk ('to uz jsem myslel, ze to vzdam'), and a mutiny section one listener skipped from its first chapter to its last without losing anything. The allocation is uneven: long on the comet, then the colony told in decades-long skips 'velmi zkratkovite', ending in what most readers call a rushed or weak close.

axis:ideas.note: About +2. A colony growing into a new civilisation ('Zamysleni nad vyvojem zcela nove civilizace z puvodnich osadniku fungovalo na jednicku'), a crowd outweighing reason, a shipboard chronicle turning a messy crash into a legend of heroes, and humanity's right to fight for its place ('jake misto jako lidstvo ve vesmiru, ci prirode zaujimame'). Dissent: derivative of Lem, Asimov and Hogan to one reader, the aliens a 'tuctovu zmes' to another.

axis:discovery.note: Partial, about +1. The comet is an unknown the crew must understand to repair and leave, and it keeps breaking expectations (a kilometre of solid ice cracking full of bubbles within a minute); its eruptions get a physical explanation one reader calls among the most original things in the book. Whether it is alive or intelligent is left open, which several readers missed ('hlavni zahada, samotny Hades, je nedoresena').

axis:multi-pov.note: Staggered: the captain carries the comet half, Ajen the colony section, with chronicle interludes and decades-long skips in the last third. One listener says it needs attention not to lose the thread; nobody describes threads starting together.

axis:sequels.note: Standalone. The last chapter opens a door to a sequel several readers asked for, but none followed: the author's only later book is her share of a multi-author anthology.

axis:infidelity.note: No reader of about seventy mentions an affair. Ajen's betrayal of Waco is political: she stages her own coup and leaves with half the crew ('podtrhla manzilkovi zidli a udelala si vlastni puc').

axis:sexual-content.note: Remove the romance and the book stands: a comet crash, repairs and a colony. The Waco and Ajen line is one thread ('Romanticka linka je spravne osudova').

axis:sexual-treatment.note: No reader in about seventy written reviews on four sites mentions a sex scene or crude content. This is absence of complaint, not a content note.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: One reader notes the 'trendu silnych emancipovanych hrdinek' and the captain overrun by his partner, but the contrast the axis prices is absent: the man is the competent one ('jak hloupe se postavy chovaji (snad krome kapitana)'), and the woman who takes power is called naive and her rule stupid.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: None in any review, discussion thread or plot summary.

axis:unearned-competence.note: One reader objects that the hero 'taha z rukavu nescetna reseni neresitelnych situaci'; the rest describe a trained navigator whose choices cost lives and are fought by the passengers, which is status earned under fire.

axis:bleakness.note: A third of the sleepers die in the crash and some readers note a dim view of crowds ('prehliadku najhorsich ludskych vlastnosti'; 'temny pocit'), but no one describes sustained hopelessness: the colony is built and the last chapter reveals what became of the other colony ships.

axis:character-differentiation.note: Divided, not priced: 'Postavy jsou dostatecne ruznorode' and a named supporting cast (the friend Davis, the hard doctor Gudrun Olafsdottir) against 'postavy plytke' and 'povrchnost postav' from audiobook listeners.

axis:opening.note: No authorized excerpt could be read (the author's webcomic site has lapsed, the archive copies were unreachable, Paseka posts no ukázka), so this rests on several independent descriptions that agree: the first scene is one room and two people, a girl turning up in a villain's lab announcing 'I'm your new Sidekick', refused until she turns into a shark. His backstory, the Institution and the joust that cost him his arm, follows within the first six pages. Some Czech readers found the gag-strip start disorienting ('pár kapitol potřebujete na zorientování'), and nothing in the log shows how a comic's first pages land with him.

axis:occult.note: How her power is conferred is left open on purpose, and no rite is staged. The only on-page conferral is a story Nimona tells in chapter 4, a fairy-tale witch in a hole who grants a wish and turns her into a dragon, which she later disowns ('What witch?'). The flashback the book does show is a sickly village girl who recovered with the power, was handed over as a 'changeling' and experimented on by the Institution. Blitzmeyer's machine cuts her off from an 'anomalous energy' studied as science, and 'dark magic' is only the label on jaderoot, a poison the Institution weaponises. The witch vignette is the one point of contact, lighter than the witch in The Chronicles of Narnia 67.

axis:detective.note: No investigation strand. Exposing the Institution is a caper and a propaganda campaign: stolen documents decoded, a fake newscast, staged poisonings. Nimona's past is a withheld personal question between two friends, not a case to solve.

axis:worldbuilding.note: Little is declared, so little is owed, and what is declared is kept. Knights alongside lasers and TV news is given from page one, not explained. The machine that blocks Nimona's shifting is set up at the Science Expo and pays off in the final fight. Her regeneration works the same way every time, and the reveal that the Director rigged the joust is planted early and paid off late. One reviewer wanted 'reasoning behind the magic system in this world (or if there even is one)', and Slate calls the book 'lumpy and oddly structured', but neither names a rule the book breaks.

axis:protagonist.note: Ballister is the kingdom's designated villain and acts against the label. He keeps rules ('Killing solves nothing... I don't kill people just because they're in my way'), calls off his poisoning scheme when two people die of it, brings the cure and is captured doing so. That is a lead moving toward good. Readers call him 'easily the most lovable “villain” in the history of books' and write 'miluju Temnotaje'. The cost is Nimona, the title character but not the viewpoint, who kills with glee and reads to some as 'childish and annoying' ('jej detinské správanie'). The book makes that the problem it argues with rather than asking anyone to cheer it.

axis:motives.note: The content is driven by motives: each lead wants something different, and the central reveal is why Goldenloin fired the lance. But the form delivers that through dialogue and faces, never narration, and the closing three of eleven chapters, half the book, go largely to a riot, a capture and a dragon rampage. Some readers found the characters flat or not given time to react ('barely get a chance to fully react'), and a Czech reader who missed relationships and emotion wrote 'film je v tomhle případě lepší než jeho předloha'. No comic in the log shows whether this reaches him.

axis:ideas.note: Nameable in one sentence: an institution that manufactures its heroes and its villains, and who gets to call someone a monster ('We assumed she was a girl disguised as a monster... She's a monster disguised as a girl'). Readers say the good-and-evil theme stayed with them and 'postavy zde nejsou jen černé, nebo bílé'. A dissenting voice calls it one idea 'který se ale rychle vyčerpá', so it earns at young-adult weight, not more.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: By the author's own account Ballister and Goldenloin were secret lovers before the joust. The book never shows a kiss and the author says 'none of the characters ever addressed it outright', but the text points to it: the Director's 'nature of your relationship' and 'fixation', Goldenloin's 'We were together. It was good', Ballister's 'Someone I love is going to try and kill her', and an epilogue that implies they are together again. Czech readers saw it ('jasný homosexuální podtext, nikdy však není nic explicitně vyřčeno'). It is the co-lead's relationship and runs through most chapters, but it is subtext and backstory, never enacted. Remove it and the rivalry and the book both stand, so this is graded, not premise: light-to-middle of the range, lighter than the enacted relationship in Čaropisci 67, and priced at about 4 points as a judgement, not a measurement.

axis:childrens.note: Small, about 2 points. It is shelved as young adult and drawn in a cartoon style. Czech readers place it at 13 and up, and one calls the dialogue 'na úrovni osemročného dieťaťa'. Against that there are gore, swearing and the deaths of many innocents, and readers say the young-adult framing does not limit it for adults. The form adds to it: the only illustrated book in the log is a short allegory, The Little Prince 82.

axis:discovery.note: No lift. The open question is Nimona's own nature, and it is not the plot's spine. The book answers it only partly, in a cell flashback, and leaves the rest open on purpose: 'it is never confirmed which scenario is the truth', and the author cut the explanations because stating anything about her as plain fact felt wrong. A withheld answer forfeits the lift, and several reviewers found the open ending frustrating.

axis:bleakness.note: It turns dark late but does not stay there. The gag-strip start gives way to 'the charm gets turned to terror quickly': the Director tortures her prisoners, and Nimona's rampage kills the Director, the King and many innocents. The close is bittersweet, not hopeless: the Institution is dismantled, Ballister and Goldenloin are reconciled, and Nimona, believed dead, smiles and waves at him from a crowd and is gone. Readers report laughing and crying, and an earlier, darker ending was rewritten.

axis:momentum.note: Read in a sitting ('incredibly fast-paced'). The early chapters are two-to-four-page gag strips and the later ones run to forty pages; one reader could not stop for the last 100 pages. The complaints run the other way from a slow book: one reader says the final quarter loses momentum, one reviewer finds the ending rushed, another 'choppy' and disjointed.

axis:density.note: No padding. About 256 pages of panels with little description, so the story is dense for its length; the faults readers name are compression and choppiness, not thinness.

axis:character-differentiation.note: Each lead thinks differently. Ballister is a rule-bound scientist, Nimona chaotic and secretive, Goldenloin vain, guilty and in the end brave ('I never did anything good my whole life... I have to TRY'), the Director bound by an oath to protect the kingdom 'no matter the cost', and Blitzmeyer an enthusiast. Readers say 'postavy zde nejsou jen černé, nebo bílé'.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: No one-sided contrast. The two cleverest characters are Ballister and Blitzmeyer, one man and one woman, both scientists. The Director is a cunning woman, and Goldenloin is a vain foil but a capable fighter, written with guilt and courage.

axis:sexual-content.note: None. A young-adult comic with no sex scenes. The only bodily jokes are a shark form drawn with breasts and Nimona mocking Goldenloin's codpiece.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Nothing crude about sex. The two sight gags above are anatomy played for slapstick, not sexual references, which is the register the reader's rule leaves alone.

axis:infidelity.note: No marriage or engagement anywhere in the plot.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Nimona's near-limitless power is given, not earned, but the book treats it as the danger it explores, not as wish-fulfilment. Ballister loses to Goldenloin again and again and builds what he has.

axis:life-phase.note: The viewpoint is Ballister, an adult the author places in his late thirties. Nimona's teenage manner is seen from outside, so it is a protagonist question, not an inner life to sit through.

axis:faith.note: Religion is never a subject. The Director wears a veil-like hood and a cross-marked badge, but the Institution is a police and heroics body and is never framed as a church.

axis:opening.note: Read in the publisher's extract of chapter one: one first-person thread in order. Family night with Daniela and Charlie, the physics career Jason gave up and the friend who kept his (Ryan's prize), the walk home, then a masked man takes him at gunpoint to a derelict power plant and drugs him ('You wouldn't believe me if I told you'). Who he is, what he loves and what he regrets are set before anything strange happens; the captor and the drug are a posed question, not missing context. Neither shape of the filter.

axis:occult.note: Power is conferred by lab work only: a box scaled up from the lead's abandoned superposition research, and a compound that, Ryan says, suppresses three regions of the prefrontal cortex, which Jason reads as switching off the observer while the box shields from outside observation. Which world a door opens on follows the traveller's emotional state, framed as the same physics. No invocation, devotion, rite or priesthood; God is a passing mention ('Brief mention of God, not major or big theme').

axis:detective.note: No investigation plot. The first act's question, what happened to me, is answered by being told (the lab staff, then Ryan), not worked out from clues, and readers guess the abductor early. A flag only because one Czech reader calls it 'scifi žánr s detektivní zápletkou'; Daniela's own chapters weigh illness, job trouble and an affair as reasons her husband has changed and decide not to look.

axis:worldbuilding.note: About four to eight points, the largest deduction. The book undertakes to explain (a compound, a shielding box, the observer effect) but hedges it as the lead's hypothesis, so the bar it sets is self-consistency. Much holds: the ampoule supply is counted down from fifty and really limits the search, the rule that feeling steers the door is set up in chapter eight and decides the last crossing, and the flood of other Jasons follows from the branching the book declared (NPR: 'completely earned'; a Czech reader of physics popularisers: 'správný a logický důsledek'). The breach is the box itself: it stands in every world they step into, including ones where nobody built it, and readers find no explanation ('Huge plot hole' in the Goodreads Q&A; at least eight Czech comments ask, 'proč se té kostky nikdo nevšiml'). Add convenience at the edges, a drugged man walking out of a guarded lab into a passing taxi and 'science a bit too convenient' (USA Today), and a recurring Czech verdict that it is a thriller 'u kterého nesmíte příliš myslet'. Peripheral to the premise, unlike Mortal Engines 55, and no declared rule is broken the way the Three Laws were in Já, robot 55, so graded, not a collapse.

axis:protagonist.note: Active, rootable and given a flaw. Jason escapes the lab on his own in chapter two, evades the pursuers in three, seeks out Daniela in five, works out the box's rules with Amanda, gets himself arrested to reach his wife and leads the endgame; only the entry into the box in chapter seven is someone else's initiative. The opposite of the passive lead Problém tří těles (DNF) was dropped on. He starts envious of the friend who kept the career and ends having chosen his life; mid-book he follows another Jason's family and later stops himself from killing another self to take his place, the direction of travel the reader rewards, not The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. Against: a minority finds him one-note ('Daniela! Daniela!' in a two-and-a-half-star Goodreads review; 'hlavní postava plochá'), and the NYT says the speed leaves no room to take stock. Ordinary is not flat and his interior is on every page, so no deduction.

axis:motives.note: One to three points; the screening's 'thin on motive' is half right. What the two Jasons want, and why, is the book's subject: one wants his family back, the other the life he gave up, argued at the climax ('we end up living in a state of perpetual regret'), and Daniela gets three chapters of her own. But the page time goes to the chase (NPR: 'one big chase scene'), the love is restated rather than explored ('laciné vyznávání lásky', 'tuny laskyplnych klise'), and the dozens of other Jasons, days-old copies, turn on the family with no reason given ('Jak mohli zaútočit na svou rodinu s úmyslem jim ublížit?').

axis:momentum.note: Fast start and constant drive, the Hunger Games 89 shape: 'almost the entire book is one big chase scene' (NPR), 'nail-biting suspense' (Philly Voice), and the commonest Czech praise is 'čtivá, svižná', many finishing it in a day or two. Dissent is a mid-book sag among the box worlds for some ('v půlce se člověk začíná lehce nudit') and predictability once the abductor is known; three of about four hundred Czech commenters say they stopped. The one-line paragraphs NPR found 'infuriating' are a style cost, not a drive one.

axis:density.note: Short (320 pages in Czech) with no description or digression to speak of. The middle complaint is repetition, worst-case worlds one after another ('proč tam nemohl být nějaký příjemný?'), not empty pages: not the uneventful stretches Problém tří těles (DNF) was dropped on.

axis:ideas.note: About two to three points. Nameable in a sentence: every choice leaves a self who chose otherwise, so what makes you you, and would you trade the life you chose for the one you did not? Jason asks aloud what the 'core components' of a self are, and the plot answers it. Czech readers keep saying it made them weigh their own crossroads ('Donutila mě ale přemýšlet o vlastním životě'); genre veterans call it familiar and shallow ('Nemá to hloubku'), and the WSJ calls it 'a meditation on personality and identity'. A modest lift, below ideas worked out at length.

axis:discovery.note: Partial, +2. Jason wakes in a world he does not understand and must understand it to get home; the box worlds are an unknown explored under a hard limit (the ampoules) with no telling what the next door holds, and the answer to who did this fits chapter one. But the central reveal comes early and many guessed it ('Ihned jsem si domyslel, kdo je únosce'), and each world is crossed rather than understood, so not the full Project Hail Mary 92 shape.

axis:infidelity.note: Below premise; priced at two to five points, and a boundary the reader should rule on. The marriage is the spine and faithful in intent: in chapter eleven Amanda gets into his bed and he sends her back, citing Daniela. But in chapter five, already suspecting this is not his world, Jason sleeps with that world's Daniela, an unmarried artist then dating Ryan; she is killed soon after. In chapter fourteen his wife asks, he says yes, she asks whether that version of her was happy, and nothing more comes of it. Prominence incidental, framing forgiven, so unpunished. If a partner who is the spouse's own other self counts as no third party, the subplot bands do not apply and it is a few points, as priced here; if the reader counts her as another woman, the rule's letter for an approving incidental moment puts the book in the 50s. One reviewer: 'Jason definitely cheated on OG Daniela, and it doesn't matter that it was another Daniela!' The impostor's night with the wife is deception, not her infidelity, and is priced under sexual-treatment.

axis:sexual-content.note: Not the plot. A handful of brief scenes in a book about getting home; no advisory or review calls sex central.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: About one to two points. Low volume, low explicitness, little crudeness: 'several open door scenes that are brief but slightly descriptive', 'a couple sex moments but nothing graphic or erotic', 'without explicit details', with f-words 'mostly used in relation to sex' in one advisory. The kind is the uneasy part: chapter four, from Daniela's side, is the impostor's night with a wife who does not know him, written as renewed passion (a reviewer: 'He's a stranger! Again, horrifying'). Válka starého muže 87 shows one chapter still registers.

axis:character-differentiation.note: About a point. The Jasons are one man by design, and the rest are thin: The Verge found Daniela and Charlie evoke little empathy and the alternate Jasons too undeveloped to remember, a book-club guide asks whether Amanda is 'merely a vehicle' for his escape, and Czech readers find Daniela accepts the impossible too easily ('si nějak snadno nechá všechno vysvětlit').

axis:multi-pov.note: Three short chapters from Daniela's side (four, six and nine), each arriving after the main thread is established; nothing starts in parallel at the opening.

axis:bleakness.note: Dark worlds are visited, not lived in: an ash-covered Chicago, a plague city where Jason gives a dying Daniela morphine at her request. The book ends with the family together opening a door on light and rain, not the 1984 60 kind.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: No competence contrast: Amanda, a psychiatrist, is capable and leaves on her own terms; Daniela gave up her art career for family as Jason gave up his science; no man is diminished to make a point.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Jason's command of the box comes from his own abandoned research, so it is earned; the easy escape from the lab is priced under worldbuilding as authorial convenience.

axis:faith.note: No religion handled; God is a passing mention.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: None in any plot summary or content advisory checked.

axis:life-phase.note: Lead about forty with a teenage son, adult interior throughout; older leads cost nothing.

readingOrder: Volume 1 of 3 of The Final Architecture (Czech series Architekti světů); read first. This volume's Czech title is Střepy Země (Planeta9/Triton 2022, transl. Milan Pohl); the cache's czTitle 'Architekti světů' is the series name, and book-series.json calls the series 'Poslední architektura', which is not the Czech name. Volume 2 Oči prázdnoty (Eyes of the Void, 2022) and volume 3 Vládci nestvůrnosti (Lords of Uncreation, 2023) are both in Czech print, Planeta9/Triton 2024. The trilogy is complete.

axis:opening.note: Read from the publisher's Czech sample (prologue and chapters 1 to 3). The prologue states the war before the scene ('V sedmdesátém osmém roce války přitáhl k Berlenhofu Architekt... Architekti totiž udeřili nejprve na Zemi') and then gives one concrete situation through Solace's eyes, a broken Intermediary dragged to the bridge who turns a moon-sized Architect, so neither shape of the filter fires. The cost is the term load: a dozen factions, ship classes and ranks named unexplained in the prologue and six crewmates introduced in chapter 2, which readers felt ('hneď od začiatku zahltí čitateľa mnohými neznámymi výrazmi', 'prvními devíti kapitolami jsem se musela vyloženě prokousávat'); about -2, eased by the book's own timeline appendix ('je naprosto nezbytne NUTNE si precist... ČASOVÁ OSA').

axis:multi-pov.note: Chapters are headed by their viewpoint ('KAPITOLA 1 SOLACE', 'KAPITOLA 2 IDRIS'): the prologue and chapter 1 are Solace, chapters 2 and 3 Idris, and the two alternate until about a third of the way in ('first alternating between Idris and a Partheni soldier named Solace, but at around the one-third mark the scope broadens'), when others join, the Mordant House agent Havaer Mundy and Kris among them. Staggered and each thread anchored first: the LOTR 84 pattern, not the Guards! Guards! (DNF) one.

axis:protagonist.note: Idris wants something concrete and keeps paying for it: to be left alone and never used as a weapon again, with no sleep since the procedure, and the sample gives him real interiority on the salvage of a refugee ship full of the dead. Critics split on whether the reluctance reads as character or passivity ('something of a pushover', 'the whining occasionally grated', 'throws tantrums a few times and can be rather annoying' against 'pečlivě zpracovaný je pouze hlavní hrdina Idris' and 'a core of steel and won't accept defeat, no matter the cost'), while Solace, the co-lead, is the one who charges in. Pushed by other people's agendas but making the deciding move at the climax, so a small cost, about -2, and not the observer shape of Problém tří těles (DNF).

axis:occult.note: The Source test passes and the mechanism escape holds: the Intermediary ability is conferred by surgery most subjects do not survive ('Prý jim řežou mozky. Tak je vyrábějí', 'Většina lidských mozků ten zákrok nevydrží'; the publisher: 'his brain twisted by surgical and chemical treatments'), and unspace is crossed with drives, not invocation or devotion. The invented faith is the Essiel Hegemony, worshipped by human colonies for a protection that really comes from Originator relics; Part Two shows on newsfeeds a consecration of a colony (a kneeling crowd, robed cultists, an Essiel processing onto the soil; seen in the novel's text through a search snippet whose host was an unlicensed copy, so not linked). That ceremony confers nothing, so it is 'light' by the stated convention, at most -2, and nothing like a sacrifice appears anywhere.

axis:detective.note: No mystery spine. The investigation-shaped strands are short and sit inside a chase: a Hiver scholar shows that a supposed Architect wreck was faked and accuses the Hegemony's cult leader of the hoax, Kris traces the cartel that hijacked the crew's ship, and Havaer Mundy's chapters are espionage pursuit. Flagged, not docked.

axis:worldbuilding.note: Declared capabilities carry visible consequences, the form the reader rewards: Earth's destruction leaves a refugee diaspora with a currency born of barter (largesse, in the sample), the relic protection makes whole colonies convert to the Hegemony, and the scarcity of Intermediaries ('Většina lidských mozků ten zákrok nevydrží') is exactly what sets the Parthenon against the human government. Readers rank it the book's strength ('the best part of the book was the world building'; aliens whose culture follows from their biology); the one reservation is that unspace is described loosely ('Unspace seemed more like magic than science').

axis:ideas.note: Aliens that turn inhabited worlds into deliberate sculpture ('Nikdo nevěděl proč, ale očividně k tomu měli nějaký důvod'), 'a threat from an intelligence that is too alien to understand', and the question of what drives them, which this volume answers in part and the trilogy in full; alongside it, worship traded for safety, eugenics and nativist hatred between human factions, and disability carried through Olli. Moderate rather than top of the log: critics find it 'played rather straight to the tropes' of space opera.

axis:discovery.note: Partial, about +2 by the stated convention: Idris has to learn what the Architects are in order to stop them, and in this volume finds he can sense Originator ruins and that the Architects are compelled by something behind them. But the spine is a chase over a relic, not the uncovering, and the full answer comes only in volume 3 of the finished trilogy; one critic found the identity of the controllers easy to guess.

axis:motives.note: The book leans on set pieces ('Akce střídá akci', 'one too many fights with indestructable aliens in a spaceship'), and a craft critic finds 'the plot accelerates too fast for any focus', leaving the crew as bit parts. Faction wants (the human government, the Parthenon, the Hegemony, a crime cartel) and Solace's split loyalty give it a spine of motive, so this is the Golden Son 92 kind of dock, somewhat larger, about -3.

axis:momentum.note: Mixed, and the cost sits in two places: the exposition-heavy first fifth ('does pick up after the first 20%'; one reader stopped there) and a sag past the middle ('getting bogged down a little past the middle', 'one third of the book was basically the crew flying from one place to another'). Most readers report the opposite ('The plot has fantastic pacing, moving quickly from set piece to set piece'), so this is not the uneventful shape that ended Problém tří těles (DNF); about -2.

axis:density.note: Long, but the plot is crowded with incident rather than thin; the complaints are front-loaded exposition and some travel, priced under momentum. Length itself costs nothing.

axis:character-differentiation.note: The crew differ by species, body and trade (a crab-like Hanni factor, a Hiver, a drone operator born without usable limbs, a duelling lawyer), but some readers found them thin ('there was so little difference in the characters' voices', 'nedošlo k žádnému velkému vývoji charakterů'). No deduction beyond the motives one.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: No same-sex romance plot found: readers say LGBTQ+ characters are present but 'these identities are not plot points', and the only romance reviews name is Solace's past with Idris, a man ('po berlenhofských událostech byli nějakou dobu spolu'). The light end applies: Solace is described as bi and flirts with Kris ('I enjoyed her flirting with Kris a bit too'), and her sisters 'tend to find romance with each other'. About -2.

axis:sexual-content.note: Nowhere near premise level: no reviewer, Czech comment or content-warning list read here mentions sexual content at all.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Innuendo only in what was found: the sample says Solace and Idris were together for a while after the battle, and an alien's lewd tone makes her blush. Medium confidence, since no full content-warning list could be read.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: The all-female Parthenon's martial edge has an in-world reason ('Uměle vytvořené válečnice', engineered for war), and competence is mixed across the sexes: Idris is the decisive power, Havaer and the captain Rollo are capable, Kris is a lawyer who duels.

axis:faith.note: Faith is a thread: the Hegemony is a political power whose human cult trades worship for safety, and its leader faking a disaster to frighten colonies in is played as politics, not as ridicule of real religion. The Crier ('Někteří ho uctívali coby posla od Boha') is explained as the last survivor of a species the Architects destroyed. Medium confidence.

axis:prophecy.note: The one foreteller is the Crier, whose warning before Earth fell is a survivor's knowledge ('Architekti se vždycky vrátí'), handled seriously.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Idris's power is paid for: a procedure few survive ('Byl jedním z mála šťastlivců, kteří ten proces přežili'), no sleep for decades, and the cost of every deep jump.

axis:bleakness.note: Grim scenes, such as a refugee hold of two hundred dead with a children's cartoon still looping in chapter 2, inside a bickering, found-family crew; not sustained grimness.

axis:sequels.note: Volume 1, read first, of a trilogy that is complete and wholly in Czech print. For the series entry: one craft critic rates volume 2 the strongest, but two Czech readers find its middle slow ('značně a zbytečně rozvleklá') and one reviewer says Idris there 'is being abducted by just about everyone', which is where the passive-lead risk lives; the same critic says volume 3 'wastes 50% of its pages going in a giant circle', while one Czech reader calls it the most action-packed of the three.

readingOrder: volume 1 of the Chaos Walking trilogy (Czech: Nespoutany chaos, Slovart, trans. Hana Brezakova): read first. It ends on a cliffhanger and continues directly into Najdi odpoved (The Ask and the Answer, vol. 2) and Probud monstrum (Monsters of Men, vol. 3), both Slovart 2019 and held in Czech print. A sequel trilogy, The New World, began in April 2026 with Piper at the Gates of Dusk, about Todd and Viola's sons twenty years on. As far as found, it is only in English.

axis:opening.note: Read in the Slovart sample of the 2018 translation. One boy and his talking dog walk to the swamp, and within three pages the book states the Noise ('od muzu a jejich myslenek, o kterych ani nevedej, ze si je myslej, kdyz je vsichni kolem muzou slyset'), the talking virus, the dead Spackle, the missing women, Ben and Cillian and the thirty days to manhood, before the chapter ends on the silence, so the filter does not fire. The cost, small at 1-3 points, is the register: the English misspelt dialect becomes colloquial Czech ('Rek sem', 'pac', 'nejni', 'cejtim') in long present-tense run-ons, and readers of both Czech translations had to get used to it ('dlooouho zvykal na tu nespisovnost'; 'Mluva Todda mi porad nesedela'), while a few never did.

axis:occult.note: The source test passes: the only power is the Noise, a contagion native to the planet that nobody invokes. The flag is depiction: Aaron, the town preacher, drugs Viola to sacrifice her to God in what study guides call a ritual, and Todd frees her before anything is done; at the climax, in a disused church behind a waterfall, Aaron tries to make Todd kill him as the sacrifice so that he becomes a saint and Todd a man, and Viola kills him to stop it. A madman's human sacrifice is attempted twice and never performed, and nothing supernatural answers it, so it is graded light (about -2) rather than vetoed, but the boundary is the reader's to rule on and he should hear of it before a proposal.

axis:detective.note: No investigation strand. Todd is told the town's secret rather than working it out: Hildy explains the germ, Ben says what the men of Prentisstown did, and Viola reads him his mother's diary.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The one declared rule holds and drives the plot: men's and animals' thoughts are audible and women's are not, Noise 'ain't the truth' because it carries wishes too, Todd's own Noise broadcasts the silence he found, pursuers track him by Noise and a waterfall masks it, and the town's crime follows from the rule (men who resented women's silence murdered them). Page one of the sample even shows how the secret was kept from Todd, a flash of 'neceho zapomenutyho' drowned by a louder sermon, and his illiteracy has an in-world cause, since the Mayor forbids reading. The earn is moderate because of the breach readers name most, in both languages: Aaron survives a crocodile mauling, a beating, a river and a torn-off nose to keep coming back ('how was Aaron not dead?'; 'the bionic man'; 'Nektere postavy byly trochu moc nesmrtelne'; 'jako certik z krabicky'), authorial rescue in reverse.

axis:protagonist.note: Interiority is total, since every page is Todd's present-tense voice, and he has flaws to overcome: a temper, the dog he cuffs on page one, and a taught hatred of the Spackle that makes him kill one and at once regret it. His direction of travel is refusal: he will not become the killer the town's rite of manhood demands, which makes him rootable. A loud minority finds him unlikeable ('vecne nastvany, sebelitostivy a protivny'; 'not exactly likable'), but what they describe is the teen temper, priced under life-phase, not flatness, and others 'loved Todd and Manchee'.

axis:motives.note: About a point. Most page time is flight, and the motives travel inside it: Todd's wish not to kill, Ben and Cillian giving everything to get him out, Viola's search for her people. The antagonists are thin, since Aaron's reasons are madness and the Mayor's plan (an army of boys made killers) arrives late and offstage, and Czech readers find the villain's recurring ambushes 'az srandovni'.

axis:ideas.note: A light earn at genre level: the Noise is information overload made literal ('Informayshun, all the time, never stopping... too much informayshun can drive a man mad'), the town's rite asks what makes a man, the knife is the choice whether to kill, and the Spackle make prejudice cost something. Ness says the gender roles were 'a way of exploring my theory about how bad we are as a species at handling difference'. Dissent: 'celek lehce povrchni', 'klouze se jen tak po povrchu'.

axis:discovery.note: Partial, about +2. Todd has never been told the truth about his own world: he thinks his town is the last, believes a germ killed the women, and does not know what becoming a man involves. He must run to stay alive, and the answers arrive in this volume and fit what was planted (a town of living women, Hildy on the germ, Ben on the history, the diary); it is only partial because he is told rather than finding out, and readers call the withholding a device ('narrative cheats'; 'jenom kvuli prodlouzeni napeti').

axis:momentum.note: The book's main strength, and close to unanimous: 'Od zacatku se leti fofrem', 'pribeh se odviji v rychlem tempu bez hluchych mist', 'jakmile jsou hlavni hrdinove na uteku, nema temer hluche misto'; in English, 'the action and suspense never lets up' and 'just one more page, just one more chapter'. Chapter one of the sample ends on a hook, and the book holds 81% from 426 databazeknih ratings. The dissent is about repetition, priced under density, plus a slow first two chapters for a few readers.

axis:density.note: A couple of points. A simple pursuit ('dej je velmi jednoduchy') runs to about 450 Czech pages, and after Todd himself the loop is the commonest complaint: 'chodi a chodi a chodi', 'zbytecne natahovane', 'epizodni situace... porad dokola a stejne', and in English it 'should have been titled The Knife of Never STOP RUNNING'. A few readers quit midway or before the last part; this is the set piece repeated for its own sake that cost Catching Fire 83.

axis:life-phase.note: Todd is twelve going on thirteen in thirteen-month years (Viola reckons him fourteen) and reads that age from the inside: he sulks, curses the dog, cries and is sure the world is against him ('radoby cool styl psani je nekdy az prehnane pubertalni'; 'stale bol nastvany'; 'Chova se jako nevzdelany kluk'). Meanwhile he and Viola act like adults, which several readers find implausible for their age. Because the whole book is his voice, this costs more than the slight Ender's Game 87 dock: two or three points.

axis:bleakness.note: A point or two. The losses pile up: Manchee is killed in front of Todd, Cillian dies, Farbranch burns, the town's history is a massacre of women and Spackle, and the book ends with Viola shot and the Mayor already ruling Haven; two Czech readers call it depressing. It is not isolation, since Todd and Viola's companionship, Manchee's loyalty and the kindness of Hildy and Tam carry it, which puts it on the Project Hail Mary 92 side of the rule rather than with 1984 60.

axis:content.note: The violence is raw for the genre ('syrove intenzivni a na pomery zanru az nezvykle krvavy'), and the dog's death is on the page: Aaron snaps Manchee's neck while Todd watches from the drifting boat. One reader calls it 'zbytecne brutalni', most call it the scene they cried at, and swearing is euphemised ('eff', with 'do haje' standing in for it in Czech), which Vector calls timid. Within the violence-and-swearing tolerance.

axis:faith.note: The preacher is the villain: Aaron quotes Scripture while beating a child, plans a sacrifice to God and seeks sainthood. It is a serious portrait of a fanatic, not satire on belief, and the book sets a kind pastor against him (Viola's ship's pastor 'was kind and gave them hope'). Faith is a thread here, never the subject, so it clears under the rule, but it is worth a line to the reader.

axis:prophecy.note: Aaron calls Viola 'the sign'. Nothing is foretold, and nobody has foreknowledge.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: Viola reads, navigates and carries her ship's technology while Todd cannot read and cannot bring himself to kill, but the book gives the reason (the Mayor forbids reading, and she grew up on a settler ship) and its cleverest mind is a man's, the Mayor's, so the competence contrast clears. What it foregrounds is a moral contrast, one town's men murdering their women for their silence, and it won the Tiptree award. Good men (Ben, Cillian, Tam) are set against that town, and Ness frames it as a story about how badly people handle difference, so the axis's object, men written as dumb, is absent.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: Ben and Cillian raise Todd together, but the text never calls them a couple and nothing romantic is on the page ('the nature of their relationship is never described in detail'). In 2021 Ness said 'In a time of all men, of course people would pair up', which only a reader who knows the interview brings to the book. The light end at most, priced at nothing.

axis:sexual-content.note: No sex. Todd is drawn to Viola and never acts on it.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Men's Noise carries sexual thoughts, which the boy narrator mentions only in passing ('The men often think about sex'). Nothing is described.

axis:infidelity.note: None. The one married couple on the page, Hildy and Tam, is a happy one.

axis:multi-pov.note: A single first-person narrator throughout ('vse vypravi jedna postava - Todd').

axis:character-differentiation.note: Todd, Viola, Ben, Cillian and Hildy are distinct, and Manchee is the best-loved member of the cast ('one of my favorite literary animal characters'; 'ten setsakramentsky pes je proste poklad'). Aaron is one-note, so the axis nets to neither earning nor costing.

axis:childrens.note: It won the Guardian Children's Fiction Prize and was written for teenagers, but nothing in it is childlike: a massacre, a rite of murder, a religious killer. Some readers place it younger ('spis pro mladsi vekove kategorie'), and the voice is priced under life-phase. A YA register cost The Hunger Games 89 nothing.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Viola's skills come from her schooling and her ship's kit, and Todd is given nothing he has not earned. Nobody is effortlessly good at everything.

axis:sequels.note: Volume 1, and it needs nothing before it. It ends on a cliffhanger (Todd carrying the shot Viola into Haven, where the Mayor is already waiting), so the arc does not close, and volumes 2 and 3 continue it directly, which the read-whole rule covers. Some Czech readers resent the open end ('tak priserny otevreny konec').
